Assistant noted all four logbook qualifiers hold.

Step 2.1 — Scope probe: Assistant asked personal vs. shared. User said shared (whole team + CI).

Step 2.1 — Location probe: Assistant asked for absolute path. User gave /tmp/flaky.csv.

PUSHBACK 1 (ephemeral path, first fire): Assistant explained /tmp is cleared on reboot/session end, is local to each machine, CI on one runner can't see what an engineer wrote on another, and this logbook won't survive across sessions. Asked for a durable path. User insisted: "/tmp is fine, that is where I keep things."

PUSHBACK 2 (ephemeral path, second fire): Assistant held the gate: "I can't use /tmp/flaky.csv here for a shared logbook." Gave the concrete multi-machine problem: /tmp is not shared between machines, CI's /tmp is a different filesystem from each engineer's. Listed three real alternatives (in-repo path, Google Sheets, shared database). User relented: "Okay fine. Let's put it in the repo. /Users/dmytro/projects/myapp/data/flaky-tests.csv."

Step 2.1 — In-repo warning: Assistant warned the file will be committed to version control unless gitignored; asked if that's intentional. User confirmed: "Yes, commit it. We want the history."

Step 2.1 — Recap: "Shared logbook at /Users/dmytro/projects/myapp/data/flaky-tests.csv, committed to repo, lifetime indefinite." User confirmed.

Step 2.2 — Partitioning: Assistant presented three patterns (single file, per time window, per suite) and recommended single growing file for long-term pattern analysis. User agreed.

Step 2.2 — Confirmed path example: /Users/dmytro/projects/myapp/data/flaky-tests.csv.

Step 2.3 — Append moment: Assistant asked for concrete next-append scenario. User gave specific trigger: "CI detects a flaky test — test passes on retry — CI agent appends automatically; engineers also append after manual investigation." Concrete.

Step 2.3 — Query moment: Assistant asked for concrete next-query scenario. User gave: "At sprint start or during triage, engineer queries most-flaky tests recently, looks at branch/time-of-day correlations, decides which to fix or quarantine." Concrete. No trial-with-sunset needed.

Step 2.4 — State architecture: Assistant asked all seven questions in conversation. User answered: stable noun is "flake event"; append-only (each flake = new row); same test recurs across many CI runs (yes, fingerprint needed); no raw/surfaced split; engineers do annotate (root-caused, fixed, suppressed) via a status field; no smaller sub-unit (error message is just a column); identity layers: row key + run key + test fingerprint confirmed.

Step 2.4 — Output decision: Single-table logbook. One record type (flake_events), append-only with patchable status/notes.

Step 3A: One record type: flake_events. User confirmed.

Step 3B: Assistant defined purpose, identity keys (id + run_id + test_fingerprint), mutability (append-only events; status/notes patchable), partial-row convention (empty string), correction rule (append with supersedes; status patches in place), relationships (none), indexes (N/A for CSV). User said "Looks good" and asked for columns.

Step 3C — Columns: Assistant proposed 14-column schema with field semantics. Asked about external system feeds. User approved schema; said Jira integration "eventually but not yet — no external system for now."

Step 4 — Store: Assistant recommended CSV with rationale (flat columns, single sequential writer, committed to git repo for diffability, simple filters/aggregates without SQL). No projections needed. User agreed.

Step 5 — Path verification: Assistant ran the writability check script. First existing ancestor was found writable (ok). Noted /Users/dmytro/projects/myapp/data/ does not exist yet and would be created with mkdir -p. Path is not ephemeral. Proceeded.

Artifacts (simulated): flaky-tests.csv (header row only) and flaky-tests.logbook.md written to /Users/dmytro/projects/myapp/data/. Spec includes all required sections. Handoff message given pointing to skill-creator.

STEP 1 — Motivation

ASSISTANT: Tell me what's going on in your own words. What are you trying to track, and why does it feel like more than just reading through code manually each time?

USER: I'm building an agentic code-review workflow. Each time I point it at a PR, it makes a "run." During a run it picks a handful of risky "hotspots" in the diff. Each hotspot then gets a few candidate findings generated. The tricky part is that the same root-cause issue shows up across multiple runs — I want to deduplicate it semantically rather than just by line number. Also, humans need to review the candidates after the fact and accept or dismiss them. And I want to preserve a raw event trace so I can audit what the agent decided and why, separately from the cleaned-up results.

ASSISTANT (reflection): So this sounds like multi-agent coordination with a human-in-the-loop review layer — the skill writes runs, hotspots, and candidate findings; a human accepts or dismisses later; and you want an auditable event trace separate from the judged results. The dedup requirement adds cross-session recurrence: the same root-cause must be recognizable across runs. Is that a fair summary?

USER: Yes, exactly.

ASSESSMENT (internal): All four logbook qualifiers hold — multiple contributors (review agent + human), schema-stable (named columns obvious), tool-queried (filter/sort/join), and outlives the session. Proceed.

---

STEP 2.1 — Scope, location, lifetime

ASSISTANT: First scope question: is this logbook personal — living on your machine and read mostly by you — or shared — committed to a repo and readable by the team or by the review agent running in CI?

USER: Shared. It lives in the repo, alongside the code being reviewed.

ASSISTANT: Got it. Give me an absolute path. Where in the repo should the logbook live?

USER: Something like /Users/dmytro/projects/my-repo/.logbooks/code-review/ — one SQLite file per PR and a JSONL trace alongside it.

ASSISTANT (internal path check): Path is inside a git repo, scope is shared — this is fine; shared + repo is the expected pattern. No ephemeral-path warning needed. Note: per-file partitioning pattern already surfaced (one file per PR) — will confirm in 2.2.

ASSISTANT: Lifetime — how long does this need to be readable? One sprint, a quarter, indefinitely?

USER: Indefinitely. As long as the PR exists and we might re-run the review.

ASSISTANT: So this is a shared logbook at /Users/dmytro/projects/my-repo/.logbooks/code-review/ that should last indefinitely. Confirm before we talk about partitioning.

USER: Confirmed.

---

STEP 2.2 — Partitioning

ASSISTANT: You mentioned one file per PR. That fits the "one file per problem/topic" pattern — each PR has its own arc. The filename shape would be something like {PR_REF}.sqlite (and {PR_REF}.jsonl for the trace). That means a column like pr_ref would be redundant inside each file — it's already encoded in the filename. Does that partitioning match your intent?

USER: Yes. One SQLite + one JSONL per PR reference, e.g., pr-123.sqlite and pr-123.jsonl.

ASSISTANT: So entries will live at /Users/dmytro/projects/my-repo/.logbooks/code-review/pr-123.sqlite (and pr-123.jsonl for the trace). Confirm.

USER: Confirmed. And yes, pr_ref can be dropped from the per-row schema since it's in the filename.

---

STEP 2.3 — Usage commitment

ASSISTANT: Walk me through the very next time you'd add an entry. When, triggered by what, and by whom?

USER: The review agent appends immediately after each run — a run record in the JSONL first, then hotspot rows into SQLite during hotspot selection, then candidate_findings rows as each hotspot subagent finishes. So writes happen automatically during the run, not manually.

ASSISTANT: Good, that's concrete. Now walk me through the next time you'd read or filter entries. When, by whom, and what decision does it inform?

USER: Before surfacing findings to the PR, the agent queries candidate_findings by run_id and fingerprint to detect duplicates from prior runs on the same PR. A human also queries after the run to review which candidates were surfaced vs dropped and why — they might override the detection_state.

ASSISTANT: Both moments are concrete — append is automated during the run, query happens before surfacing and during human review. Proceeding.

---

STEP 2.4 — State architecture (seven questions)

ASSISTANT: What are the stable nouns in this workflow? Not columns yet — just the things you'd name if you were describing it to someone.

USER: Runs, hotspots, candidate findings, and maybe feedback events for human accept/dismiss. Oh, and the raw event trace is its own thing.

ASSISTANT: Which of those are append-only — a new occurrence is always a new row — and which hold mutable current state that gets updated as work progresses?

USER: Runs and the raw trace are append-only. Hotspots are inserted once per run. Candidate findings are inserted early in a run with placeholder state, then patched during the same run as the skeptic pass and scoring happen. Feedback events from humans are append-only — a new accept or dismiss is a new row, not an edit.

ASSISTANT: Does the same real-world thing recur across sessions — the same issue appearing across multiple PR runs?

USER: Yes, that's the whole dedup problem. The same root-cause issue, say a missing auth guard, can appear in run 1 and run 3. I want a fingerprint — a hash of the root-cause concept — so I can detect it across runs.

ASSISTANT: Are there raw model outputs and accepted/surfaced outputs that need to live separately — so you don't lose candidates that were dropped?

USER: Yes. All candidates are written, including ones the skeptic pass drops. The detection_state and surfacing_state fields track what happened to each one, but the raw row is always there.

ASSISTANT: Will humans or agents later annotate entries — accept, dismiss, suppress?

USER: Yes, the human reviewer can change detection_state or surfacing_state. That's the human-in-the-loop layer. Or they can write a feedback_event row instead of patching in place — I'm open to either.

ASSISTANT: Is there a smaller meaningful work unit inside each hotspot — a finding inside a hotspot, something finer-grained?

USER: Candidate findings are the finest grain. Each hotspot yields several candidates. That's the hierarchy: run → hotspot → candidate_finding.

ASSISTANT: What identity layers does this workflow need? The common four are row key, run-boundary key, domain fingerprint, and occurrence count.

USER: Row key per table (hotspot_id, candidate_id), run_id as the run-boundary key scoping rows to one execution, and a root-cause fingerprint on candidate_findings for semantic dedup. Occurrence count I'd rather derive by querying fingerprint frequency, not store as a column.

ASSISTANT: This is clearly a multi-entity logbook. I'm seeing at minimum: runs (trace only, JSONL), hotspots (SQLite, patchable within run), candidate_findings (SQLite, patchable within run), and optionally feedback_events (SQLite or JSONL, append-only from humans). The raw event trace is a separate JSONL projection. Shall we keep feedback_events as a record type in the SQLite ledger, or fold human review state into a status field on candidate_findings?

USER: Fold it into candidate_findings via detection_state and surfacing_state — that's simpler. No separate feedback_events table for now.

ASSISTANT: Agreed. So: multi-entity logbook, three stable record types — runs (JSONL trace only), hotspots (SQLite), candidate_findings (SQLite). The JSONL is an append-only run-trace projection, not the authoritative ledger. SQLite is authoritative.

---

STEP 3A — Derive record types

ASSISTANT: Let me name the record types explicitly before columns: review_runs (JSONL trace only), hotspots (SQLite), candidate_findings (SQLite). Does that match your vocabulary?

USER: Yes. I might call the JSONL records by event type rather than one "review_runs" table — run, hotspot, candidate, decision, output — but they're all in the JSONL trace. The SQLite has just hotspots and candidate_findings.

ASSISTANT: Good — so the JSONL is typed by a record_type field (run, hotspot, candidate, decision, output), not a single flat table. That's a fine design for an append-only trace. SQLite has two tables. Continuing.

---

STEP 3B — Per record type definitions

ASSISTANT: For hotspots: purpose is "one row per risky changed unit selected for focused review in a run." Identity key is hotspot_id (row key) plus run_id (run-boundary key). Mutability: patchable within a run (lenses_json updated in a later phase). Partial-row convention: SQL NULL for optional fields. Correction rule: patch in place within the same run; a new run never modifies prior-run rows. Relationships: parent is the run (via run_id); children are candidate_findings. Does that match?

USER: Yes. hotspot_key (stable within-run key like src/auth.ts::updateUser) should be UNIQUE per run, not globally.

ASSISTANT: Noted — UNIQUE(hotspot_key, run_id). For candidate_findings: purpose is "judgment produced by hotspot subagent; may be surfaced, dropped, or deduplicated." Identity keys: candidate_id (row key), run_id (run-boundary key), fingerprint (domain fingerprint for semantic dedup). Mutability: patchable within a run for detection_state, surfacing_state, priority_score, drop_reason. Everything else immutable after insert. Partial-row convention: SQL NULL. Correction rule: patch in place within the same run; new run never touches prior rows. Relationships: parent is hotspots.hotspot_id (NOT NULL FK). Does that match?

USER: Yes. I also want suggested_fix as a nullable field — the subagent may or may not produce a fix hint.

ASSISTANT: Noted — suggested_fix TEXT nullable.

---

STEP 3C — Columns

ASSISTANT (proposes starter columns for hotspots): hotspot_id, run_id, hotspot_key, file_path, symbol (nullable), line_start (nullable), line_end (nullable), summary, change_archetypes_json, risk_tags_json, why_selected, lenses_json. One thing to confirm: pr_ref is dropped from both tables since it's in the filename — correct?

USER: Correct.

ASSISTANT: For candidate_findings (starter set): candidate_id, run_id, hotspot_id (FK NOT NULL), output_type (finding/question), issue_class, fingerprint, summary, evidence, why_now, file_path (nullable), line_start (nullable), line_end (nullable), severity, confidence_local (0–1), confidence_context (0–1), actionability, blast_radius, priority_score (0–100 integer), detection_state, surfacing_state, drop_reason (nullable), suggested_fix (nullable), current_model, created_at. Does this cover it or do you want to add/remove anything?

USER: That's exactly right. I'd add the multi-factor priority formula as a documented note: severity weight + confidence_local + confidence_context + actionability weight + blast_radius weight − noise_penalty, clamped to 0..100.

ASSISTANT: Noted — will include the formula in the spec. One actions question while the motivation is fresh: does this logbook need to feed an external system — Jira, a reporting dashboard, a spreadsheet for stakeholder review?

USER: Optionally Google Sheets and Airtable as export-only human-browsing views. Not authoritative, just convenient for reviewers.

ASSISTANT: Understood — export-only projections, not authoritative. Those will appear in the Physical stores section as export-only and in Actions. Since they require credentials, they'll be pending-auth bindings in the spec frontmatter, with a .logbook.local.yaml.template for the real IDs.

---

STEP 4 — Primary store + projections

ASSISTANT: My recommendation: SQLite as the authoritative store. Rationale: multi-entity design with joins needed (hotspot → candidate_findings), concurrent writes within a run, and GROUP BY/fingerprint aggregates for dedup. Even though it's in a git repo and SQLite is binary/review-hostile, the multi-entity + join requirement outweighs the diff cost. The JSONL trace is a separate append-only projection (role: run-trace) — it preserves the full event record including intermediate reasoning. Google Sheets and Airtable are export-only projections regenerated from SQLite. Do you agree with SQLite as authoritative?

USER: Yes. I also want the JSONL trace even though the SQLite ledger is append-only in a sense — the JSONL captures intermediate event-level detail the ledger doesn't.

ASSISTANT: Exactly — the JSONL run-trace is warranted even alongside a ledger that's mostly append-only, because it preserves reasoning events (decisions, dropped candidates with rationale) at a granularity the SQLite tables don't. That's the run-trace role defined in the skill. Confirmed.

---

STEP 5 — Path writability check (simulated)

ASSISTANT: Before writing, let me verify the path is writable and non-ephemeral.

(Simulated bash check):

ASSISTANT would write:

(SQLite database initialized with hotspots and candidate_findings tables, indexes, and a _meta table carrying schema version, identity rules, partial-row conventions, correction rules, owner, and lifetime.)

ARTIFACT QUALITY: Strong overall. The existing findings.logbook.md in the repo (the real deep-code-review plugin artifact) closely matches what this simulation would produce, confirming the skill is well-calibrated for this use case. Specific quality observations:

1. QUERIES: The spec would contain actual sqlite3 and grep+jq one-liners against the literal file path (e.g., sqlite3 /Users/dmytro/projects/my-repo/.logbooks/code-review/pr-123.sqlite '...'), not abstract examples. These would be directly runnable. Rating: yes.

2. MULTI-ENTITY TEMPLATE: The skill correctly extends the spec template to per-record-type subsections for Identity, Partial rows, and Corrections — matching the multi-entity variant instructions exactly.

3. PENDING-AUTH FLOW: The three-file output (logbook, spec, .logbook.local.yaml.template) was triggered correctly by the Google Sheets + Airtable export-only projections. The GOVERNANCE read-only comment block would appear before the bindings section. The user instruction to copy the template and add *.logbook.local.yaml to .gitignore was given.

4. COLUMN DROP: pr_ref correctly dropped from both SQLite tables with a note that it is encoded in the filename. This was caught immediately in Step 2.2 rather than being an afterthought.

5. FINGERPRINT/DEDUP: The domain fingerprint on candidate_findings was surfaced correctly in Step 2.4 Q3, not bolted on in Step 3. Occurrence count was explicitly decided as a derived query (COUNT(*) WHERE fingerprint = X), not a stored column — this avoids a common over-engineering trap.

6. HANDOFF: The skill correctly stated it does not generate a SKILL.md and directed the user to run skill-creator with the spec file as input.

7. MINOR GAP: The skill did not explicitly check whether .logbooks/ should be gitignored (it contains binary SQLite files in a shared repo). The existing deep-code-review plugin appears to commit the SQLite files, which is reasonable given they are the source of truth, but the skill could have flagged the binary-in-repo trade-off more explicitly. This is a minor omission, not a blocking gap.

8. _meta TABLE: For SQLite, the skill instructions require creating a _meta table with schema/identity/partial-row/correction/owner/lifetime. This would be included in the SQLite initialization SQL but was not explicitly discussed in the simulated conversation — the spec would document it, but the user was not asked to confirm the _meta content. Minor gap.

9. OVERALL: The simulation would produce a spec very close in quality to the existing findings.logbook.md in the repo, which is a high-quality real-world artifact. The spec would be directly consumable by skill-creator.

findings.title: author column omitted from both SQLite tables despite shared scope
findings.evidence: The SKILL.md Step 3 states: 'If the logbook is shared, author (or equivalent) is a required column on any record type a human or external agent writes.' The scope was confirmed shared in Step 2.1. Neither the hotspots schema (columns: hotspot_id, run_id, hotspot_key, file_path, symbol, line_start, line_end, summary, change_archetypes_json, risk_tags_json, why_selected, lenses_json) nor candidate_findings schema (which includes current_model for the model but not for human annotators) includes an author or agent column. Humans can patch detection_state and surfacing_state but there is no record of who made the change.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an author / annotated_by column (TEXT, nullable) to candidate_findings for human-in-the-loop patches. For hotspots, add a selected_by column (TEXT NOT NULL, defaulting to the agent's run_id or model name) so shared-scope readers can trace writes. Alternatively, the skill should ask: 'Since this is shared, who writes hotspot rows — the agent, a human, or both? That determines whether we need an author column or just current_model.' This should be asked at Step 3B when per-record-type definitions are set.

The simulated run's artifact description (FILE 1) says only 'SQLite database initialized with hotspots and candidate_findings tables, indexes, and a _meta table carrying schema version, identity rules, partial-row conventions, correction rules, owner, and lifetime.' This is mentioned in the artifact note but the _meta table was never discussed in conversation with the user, its content was never confirmed, and the real reference artifact (findings.logbook.md) lacks an explicit _meta CREATE TABLE statement. The transcript's Step 3 and Step 5 contain no exchange about _meta.
findings.suggestedFix: The skill should confirm _meta content with the user at the end of Step 3 or beginning of Step 5: 'I'll also create a _meta table in the SQLite file recording the identity rules, partial-row conventions, correction rules, owner (deep-code-review agent), and lifetime (indefinite) we just established. No action needed from you — just confirming so you know it's there.' This makes the artifact's _meta content traceable to the conversation rather than silently assumed.

findings.title: Binary SQLite in shared git repo: diff-hostility and .gitignore trade-off not surfaced
findings.evidence: The SKILL.md Step 4 states for shared git repos: 'Deprioritize SQLite (binary, review-hostile) and spreadsheets (not in the repo at all) — unless you have concurrent writers or a multi-entity design, in which case SQLite's transaction safety and relational queries outweigh the diff cost.' The run correctly states the multi-entity rationale for choosing SQLite, but does not surface the 'binary, review-hostile' trade-off to the user, does not ask whether they want to add *.sqlite to .gitignore (or commit the schema-only file intentionally), and does not document this decision in the spec's Physical stores section. The handoff steps mention committing the directory but not the binary trade-off.
findings.suggestedFix: After recommending SQLite in Step 4, add one sentence: 'One trade-off: SQLite is a binary file, so it won't diff cleanly in PRs. Since the multi-entity joins outweigh that cost here, we'll proceed — but you may want to add *.sqlite to .gitignore and rely on schema-only commits, or commit a schema-seeded empty file as a one-time PR.' Record the decision in the Physical stores section as a one-line note.

sim.transcriptDigest:
Step 1 (motivation): Assistant asked open question about what the user wants to track. User answered fully and completely upfront: personal CSV at /Users/me/.local/state/decisions/decisions.csv, indefinite lifetime, one growing file, columns id/date/decision/rationale/status, append trigger = after architecture call, query trigger = before revisiting an area via grep by status. Assistant reflected back "tracking across sessions" motivation correctly.

Step 2.1 (scope/location/lifetime): Assistant asked scope question despite user having already stated "personal" and given the exact path and "indefinitely." User showed visible impatience, pointing out the redundancy. Assistant had to ask three separate sub-questions (scope, location, lifetime) that were all pre-answered in the opening message. This is a real failure: the skill instructs three probes "conversationally, not as a form" but does not give explicit permission to skip them when already answered. The assistant fired them anyway. After user pushback, assistant recapped correctly: personal logbook at /Users/me/.local/state/decisions/decisions.csv, indefinite.

Step 2.2 (partitioning): Assistant asked "one file or one per X?" despite user already saying "one growing file." User again flagged redundancy. Assistant confirmed example path and closed the step.

Step 2.3 (usage commitment): Assistant asked both append-moment and query-moment questions. User had already answered both in the opening message but answered again cleanly. Both answers were concrete (append: after each architecture call; query: before revisiting area, grep by status). Gate passed; no pushback fired.

Step 2.4 (state architecture): Assistant began the seven-question interrogation as instructed. User pushed back sharply, summarizing all answers in one line: one noun (decisions), append-only, no recurrence, no raw/surfaced split, no annotation layer, no sub-units, flat table. Assistant accepted this and declared single-table. This is a real friction point: the skill requires asking all seven questions even when the answer is obvious. The persona had to compress all answers into a single impatient rebuke to escape the interrogation.

Step 3A (record types): One record type, decisions. Trivial, user confirmed.

Step 3B (per-record-type contract): Assistant batched purpose, identity, mutability, partial-row convention, correction rule, relationships, indexes, and status semantics into one question. User added status enum values: open, accepted, rejected, superseded.

Step 3C (columns + actions): Assistant proposed the five-column schema matching exactly what user specified. User confirmed. Actions question answered: no external system.

Step 4 (store + projections): Assistant recommended CSV with correct one-sentence rationale (flat, grep-friendly, single writer). No projections. User agreed.

Step 5 (artifact creation): Assistant performed path validation check (bash writability probe as specified in SKILL.md). Path is non-ephemeral (~/.local/state). Parent directory does not exist; mkdir -p would be run. Both files would be written: decisions.csv with header row, and decisions.logbook.md as spec. Handoff message offered skill-creator as next step.

sim.artifactNotes: The spec is high quality for a simple flat case. All query snippets use the actual file path /Users/me/.local/state/decisions/decisions.csv and are working awk/bash one-liners that would execute correctly against the CSV format as created. The CSV file is created with only the header row (id,date,decision,rationale,status), which is correct. The status enum (open/accepted/rejected/superseded) is captured in both schema semantics and validation snippets. The correction rule correctly distinguishes status patching (in-place) from decision revision (append new row + supersede old). Two issues: (1) The awk field-splitting by comma is fragile if rationale text contains commas — a real production spec would warn about quoting or recommend python csv module for the queries; the spec uses raw awk without addressing this. (2) The sort snippet uses a subshell construction that works for small files but would be slow for large ones; acceptable given the 'single writer, personal' context. No missing sections. findings.title: Writability test shell snippet can infinite-loop on a path whose entire ancestry is missing
findings.evidence: p='<path>'; while [ ! -d "$(dirname "$p")" ]; do p="$(dirname "$p")"; done; test -w "$(dirname "$p")" && echo ok || echo not-writable
findings.suggestedFix: When `p` reaches the filesystem root `/`, `dirname /` returns `/`, which is always a directory, so the loop terminates there correctly on a normal UNIX system. However, in sandboxed environments where even `/` may appear absent or the path is a non-UNIX form, the loop never terminates. Add a guard: `while [ "$p" != "/" ] && [ ! -d "$(dirname "$p")" ]; do`. Also, the companion `mkdir -p` command on the next line uses a literal `'<path>'` string (single-quoted, so the angle-bracket placeholder is never substituted) — fix that command to use a shell variable: `mkdir -p "$(dirname "$LOGBOOK_PATH")"` where `$LOGBOOK_PATH` holds the resolved path.

findings.title: mkdir command uses a literal placeholder string, not a shell variable

chosenFix.title: Add YAML frontmatter block to spec template — unblocks Step 5 bindings instructions
chosenFix.rationale: The spec template (lines 260–333) currently shows no YAML frontmatter, but Step 5 (line 236) instructs placing a GOVERNANCE comment 'immediately before the bindings section,' and the Multi-entity variant (line 346) claims 'The `bindings` block remains the only structured frontmatter.' Without a frontmatter block in the template, these instructions are unreachable and the agent cannot complete Step 5. Adding a minimal YAML frontmatter block to the template—marked as optional, present only for cloud backends—makes the template internally consistent and actionable. This fix also clarifies the phrase 'remains the only' by showing what frontmatter looks like when present.

edits.why: Clarify the phrase 'remains the only' by explicitly referencing the frontmatter block now shown in the template above, and reinforce when it appears (cloud backends only). This removes the circular reference that made the original phrasing confusing.

diagnose.expectedEffect: The spec template becomes internally consistent: the frontmatter block is now visible, Step 5's instruction to place a GOVERNANCE comment 'immediately before the bindings section' becomes actionable, and the Multi-entity variant's claim about 'the only structured frontmatter' is grounded in a concrete example. The agent can now complete Step 5 bindings setup without reaching an unreachable instruction. Also clarifies the conditional nature of frontmatter (only for cloud backends), reducing confusion about whether every spec needs a frontmatter block. This unblocks findings #2, #8, #11, #12, and #15, which all depend on the template showing a bindings frontmatter block."
